title: Runs of Consecutive Numbers Summing to N
statement:
You get a positive integer n. Count the ways to write n as a sum of one or more consecutive positive integers, like 4 + 5 + 6.

A run of length 1 (just n itself) counts. Two ways are different when they use a different set of numbers.

examples.why: Only 16 itself. 16 has five divisors, so "count the divisors" is the wrong idea: no run of 2, 4, 8 or 16 numbers works.
21, 10 + 11, 6 + 7 + 8 and 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6. Note the run of 6 numbers: an even length can work too.

hints: A run of k numbers starting at a has sum k·a + k(k−1)/2. Which k can possibly work?
Fix the length k. Then a = (n − k(k−1)/2) / k must be a positive whole number. That gives one check per k.
Since k(k−1)/2 < n, k is at most about √(2n). Loop over k only up to there, so the work is O(√n), not O(n).

explain.intuition:
Stop thinking about where a run starts. Think about how long it is. A run of k numbers starting at a is a + (a+1) + … + (a+k−1) = k·a + k(k−1)/2. So for a fixed length k, the start is forced: a = (n − k(k−1)/2) / k. The run exists exactly when that is a whole number of at least 1.

The triangle part k(k−1)/2 grows like k²/2, and it must stay below n. So only lengths up to about √(2n) matter: around 45 000 checks for a billion, instead of a billion start points.
steps: If rest is divisible by k, a run of length k exists: add 1.
pitfalls: Looping over every start point up to n. With n near a billion that is far too slow.
Allowing a start of 0 or a negative start. rest must stay strictly positive, which is why the loop condition is <, not ≤.
Assuming only odd lengths work. 10 + 11 has length 2. The odd-divisor shortcut counts odd divisors of n, not odd lengths.

solutions.title: Try every start
solutions.idea: For each start, add consecutive numbers until the sum reaches or passes n.

solutions.title: Loop over the run length
solutions.idea: For length k the start is (n − k(k−1)/2) / k. Count the k where that is a positive integer; k never exceeds about √(2n).

solutions.title: Count odd divisors
solutions.idea: Each way corresponds to exactly one odd divisor of n. Strip the factors of 2, then count divisors of what is left by trial division.

followups: Why does each way match exactly one odd divisor of n? Pair the run length with the odd part of 2n.
Return the runs themselves, shortest first, instead of the count.
